column1: # Montana call signs — the rows are chosen one by one; the picker covers the WHOLE list.
# WHAT IT IS. A person who has claimed no name is still a person, and an address is not a way to
# call one. Seven bits taken from an account reference pick one row here, and that row is what the
# person is called until they claim a name of their own. Nobody issues it, nowhere is it
# registered, and it costs nothing to carry.
# IT IS A CALL SIGN, NOT A NICKNAME. A nickname a person picks, and it is then about who they wish
# to seem. A call sign is given, and it simply is — like height, like a date of birth — and there
# is nothing in it to be shy of. Every rule of admission below serves that one feeling:
#   nothing domesticated and nothing man-made — nobody belongs to anyone, and no state made it;
#   no young and no diminutive — there is nothing here to coo over;
#   no prey — a living row either hunts or is left alone, the swan and the elephant included;
#   no god, no hero, no country — no culture may say "this one is ours", and no row here can
#     insult anyone;
#   one word, no ornament — a tiger and a storm weigh the same, they are merely dangerous in
#     different ways.
# What the set says to the person wearing it: you are not named something sweet and you are not
# named something frightening — you are named something that was on this earth long before any
# state and answers to nobody: a beast, a weather, a light in the sky, a stone.
# IT DOES NOT TELL PEOPLE APART, AND IT IS NOT MEANT TO. With this many rows, two people out of any
# twenty will share a call sign, and that is not a defect: telling apart is what the address is
# for, and a name is what the name layer is for. A call sign answers one question only — how to
# address someone whose address you already hold.
# THE ADJECTIVE IS THE PERSON'S OWN. A second frozen list would double the surface the set has to
# hold identical everywhere, would demand a translation in every language with gender agreement in
# some of them, and would still not turn a label into an identifier. So there is no second list:
# a person may put a word of their own in front of their call sign — any word, any language, as
# long or as short as they like — and that word is theirs, not the set's. It is not derived, not
# frozen, not agreed between implementations, and an implementation that ignores it stays correct.
# This is also the only choice a call sign allows, and it is deliberately the person's.
# The Russian gender column exists for that word alone: a Russian adjective agrees with the noun,
# and without the column a person would write "Могучий Рысь". Languages that do not inflect ignore
# it.
# FROZEN. This list is a quantity of the set: every implementation of Montana holds it byte for
# byte, in this order, because the order IS the index. Moving a row renames every unnamed person at
# once; the set changes only by the author's word, and such a change knowingly reshuffles derived
# call signs. Correcting a translation is allowed; the English
# column is the source and the only part the derivation depends on.
# The rules yielded the core of the list; rows are appended at the tail and removed by the
# author's word, with the index renumbered in place. Padding a list up to a round number is how
# a rule turns into a decoration.
# columns: index<TAB>en<TAB>ru<TAB>ru_gender<TAB>zh-Hans
